d: Safety in agreement: the property that all correct non-faulty processes decide on the identical value, ensuring no divergence among behaving participants.
Validity in agreement: the decided value must have been proposed by some process in the system, guaranteeing agreements are grounded in actual proposals.
Integrity in agreement: no process decides more than once, or if it decides twice it decides the same value both times, preventing duplicate or inconsistent decisions.
Termination in agreement: every correct process eventually decides some value, ensuring the protocol makes progress and does not stall indefinitely.
Uniform agreement: all processes including those that later fail must decide on the same value, stricter than ordinary agreement which only binds correct processes.
Total order in agreement: decisions form a linearizable sequence such that all processes observe decisions in the same global order.
Quorum in agreement: a subset of processes sufficient to guarantee agreement can be reached, typically intersecting any valid quorum to ensure overlap.
Threshold in agreement: the minimum number of correct processes required to guarantee safety and liveness under given failure assumptions.
Asymmetric agreement: one class of processes (e.g., primary) must agree while another class (e.g., backups) may reach different decisions, used in primary-backup protocols.
Crash recovery agreement: agreement property that persists across process crashes and restarts, requiring recovered processes to rejoin with correct state.
View change agreement: agreement maintained during membership changes when processes join, leave, or are suspected failed, requiring re-establishment of quorums.
Architecture where all replicas process requests independently with deterministic execution.

The property that a set of distributed processes reach the same decision outcome on a given value. Uniform agreement requires all processes including those that later crash to decide identically; asymmetric agreement permits different decision classes for different process roles such as primary versus backup.
A proposal that fails to collect a quorum of accepts is abandoned, allowing the proposer to retry with a higher proposal number.
A node records a received proposal, typically after verifying the proposal number exceeds any previously promised or accepted number, committing the node to vote for that value.
The second phase of a two-phase agreement protocol wherein the proposer sends accept messages containing the proposal number and value; recipients accept if the number meets their promise.
The act of durably recording a decided value in the log or state machine, making it irreversible under correct-node behavior.
A value reaches agreement when a quorum of nodes have accepted it; once decided, the value is stable and no correct process will adopt a conflicting value.

A logical time boundary in epoch-based consensus; a leader is established per epoch and all proposals within the epoch are totally ordered, with epoch changes providing safety despite leader failures.
A node acquires knowledge of a decided value, typically by receiving accept acknowledgements from a quorum or by notification from a leader that the value has been committed.

The first phase of a two-phase agreement protocol wherein a proposer requests permission to propose by sending a prepare message with a proposal number; recipients promise not to accept lower-numbered proposals and report any previously accepted value.
A commitment from a node that it will not accept proposals with numbers lower than the promised threshold; it may carry a previously accepted value to preserve when the new proposal number wins.
A totally ordered identifier attached to a proposal, used to break ties and ensure the most recent proposal wins; typically a (round, node_id) pair.
A node submits a value for consideration by the agreement protocol; the proposed value carries a proposal number for ordering and is broadcast to quorum-forming peers.
The minimal set of nodes whose responses are sufficient to guarantee agreement; in majority-quorum systems this is any set intersecting all majorities, preventing split-brain divergence.
The cast support of a node for a particular proposal, recorded and counted toward quorum; votes are durable and prevent re-opening decided values.
Repair of divergent replicas by comparing Merkle trees and exchanging differences.
Raft RPC used for log replication and as heartbeat between leader and followers.
Index of highest log entry applied to the local state machine.

Failure detection: the capability of a distributed system to observe and identify when a process or component has stopped responding or exhibited faulty behavior, typically via timeout mechanisms or heartbeat protocols.

Failure classification: categorization of failure modes including crash failure where a process halts, omission failure where messages are lost, and Byzantine failure where arbitrary or malicious behavior occurs.
Redundancy: the duplication of critical components data or processing capacity so that system operation can continue when some components fail.
Replication factor: the configured number of replica copies of data maintained across distinct processes to survive loss of some copies while preserving availability and consistency.
Failover: the automated process of transferring operation from a failed primary component to a designated backup replica without human intervention.
Availability: the degree to which a distributed system remains operational and accessible over time despite component failures, often expressed as a proportion of uptime.

Partition tolerance: the property that a distributed system continues to operate correctly even when network communication between nodes is delayed or severed, splitting the system into isolated components.

Recovery: the procedures and protocols by which a distributed system restores consistent state after detecting and isolating a failure, including log replay and state reconstruction from replicated_log.
Failure masking: the ability of a system to conceal the effects of component failures from users by using redundancy and automatic recovery so that failures appear invisible.
Liveness preservation: maintaining the termination property of consensus a004 so that the system continues to make progress even as components fail and recover.
Safety preservation: maintaining the uniform agreement property a005 so that all processes including failed ones decide the same value despite partial failures.
Quorum reconfiguration: dynamically adjusting the quorum size a007 required for consensus operations as processes join leave or fail, while preserving overlap guarantees.
Threshold adaptation: modifying the minimum correct processes a008 needed for safety and liveness as the membership of the distributed system changes.
Leader election: the process of selecting a new primary process to coordinate consensus operations when the current leader fails, often requiring failure detection ft001 and quorum agreement.
Crash recovery: the restart procedure by which a failed process rejoins the replicated_log after recovery, potentially requiring state synchronization from remaining correct replicas.
Byzantine fault tolerance: the ability to maintain consensus and safety properties even when some processes exhibit arbitrary or malicious behavior, extending beyond simple crash failure models.
CAP theorem implications: the inherent tradeoffs between consistency consensus and availability ft006 and partition tolerance ft007 that fault tolerance designs must navigate.
